newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: China concerned over U.S. military - Australia.
newsitem.headline: China concerned over U.S. military - Australia.

text.p: China, seeking to boost its own military role in the Asia-Pacific, has expressed concern about the continued heavy U.S. military presence in the region, Australian Defence Minister Ian McLachlan said on Friday.
McLachlan told reporters Beijing disagreed with Canberra's policy that a continuing strong U.S. force boosted regional security.
"We believe that the position of the Americans being in Japan is better for everybody, including them," McLachlan said.
"I think it's fair to say they probably disagree with that position. Our view won't change. Their's may not either. It's a matter of discussion, it's not a matter of great warmth."
But McLachlan stressed Beijing did not see the U.S. force as either a threat or an attempt to contain an economically and militarily resurgent China.
Washington has about 100,000 soldiers in the region, mainly in Japan and South Korea, and maintains a strong naval and air presence.
Japan and Australia have recently boosted defence cooperation with the United States, prompting some criticism from Chinese commentators.

But McLachlan said China had assured Australia in top level official talks that it had no problems with the strengthened Washington-Canberra ties under Australia's 15-month-old conservative Liberal-National government.
The talks were part of a series of meetings between top level defence officials, diplomats and ministers between the two countries.
Neighbouring southeast Asian countries saw the pact simply as cementing a continued U.S. security role, he said.
"The Chinese don't necessarily agree. But nevertheless, they don't, as I say, regard those arrangements as either a threat or part of a China-containment conspiracy."
The United States said last month it had enough forces in the region to handle any flare up in tension and to ensure rival countries settled disputes peacefully.
Commander of the U.S. Navy in Japan, Rear Admiral Michael Haskins, told a Singapore defence conference that the U.S. role was to "deter the rise of any hegemonistic power or coalition" in the region.
China, funding a military modernisation programme from its runaway economic growth, is embroiled in several territorial disputes with regional powers.
China's military build-up and territorial claims have prompted concerns among regional governments and warnings of potential conflict.
